headline: MISSED CATCH-UP (Sat Oct 24, in no prior scan) -- Beijing firmly opposes US Treasury proposal to expand outbound investment curbs
dek: China's commerce ministry on Saturday urged the US to stop expanding restrictions on American investments in China, calling the US Treasury's proposed rule 'discriminatory', saying it widened China-related curbs and intensified them, damaged bilateral economic ties, ran counter to the consensus…
sources: Chinese commerce ministry statement via Reuters; US Treasury proposal via AP
fault_line: National-security capital controls vs market openness: does blocking US money from Chinese biotech/AI protect security, or push the tech race into a subsidy war that hurts US firms too?

sections.what_happened: China's commerce ministry on Saturday urged the US to stop expanding restrictions on American investments in China, calling the US Treasury's proposed rule 'discriminatory', saying it widened China-related curbs and intensified them, damaged bilateral economic ties, ran counter to the consensus reached by the two presidents (who have met twice in six months), and reserving the right to take unspecified countermeasures. The Treasury proposal (Thursday Oct 22, implementing the Dec 2025 Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act) adds biotechnology to restricted sectors and expands coverage of high-performance computing and hypersonic systems, on top of existing curbs on semiconductors, quantum technologies and AI; it applies to investments above $50,000, excludes most public stock purchases, takes public comments until Dec 7, 2026, with final regulations due March 2027. The proposal also extends to other 'countries of concern' (Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia).
sections.what_verified: Beijing's statement carried by Reuters (T1); the Treasury proposal independently reported by AP (T1, via Business Standard/Hindu BusinessLine); Beijing's position also carried via Xinhua (T3, STATE CN) through SANA. Three distinct publisher families.
sections.what_disputed: Treasury says the measures are not China-only and aim to stop US capital supporting foreign adversaries' dual-use strategic technologies. Beijing's 'discriminatory' characterisation is its own position, not an adjudicated fact. The proposal is draft only: comments run to Dec 7, 2026 and no new restriction is in force yet beyond the existing program (in force since Jan 2025).
sections.why_matters: Beijing just drew a red line around America's money: the Treasury wants US cash out of Chinese biotech and hypersonics, and China says it will answer — but nothing is law yet.
sections.context: Background: MISSED CATCH-UP (Sat Oct 24, in no prior scan) -- Beijing firmly opposes US Treasury proposal to expand outbound investment curbs to biotech, hypersonics and supercomputing

totw_analysis: Our read: Beijing just drew a red line around America's money: the Treasury wants US cash out of Chinese biotech and hypersonics, and China says it will answer — but nothing is law yet. The fault line our audience is arguing over: National-security capital controls vs market openness: does blocking US money from Chinese biotech/AI protect security, or push the tech race into a subsidy war that hurts US firms too?
